library: NASA satellite library (Climate Claim on Trial)

grid.tiles: 6 x 12 tiles of 30 x 30 cells; tile r covers 90-30r N to 60-30r N, tile c covers 180W+30c eastward
grid.encoding: gunzip; bytes = [all high bytes of the int16 values][all low bytes]; int16 little-endian = (high<<8)|low; layout [month][30][30]; value = int16*scale + offset; -32768 = no data; tiles that are entirely no-data are not written

variables.name: Precipitation (rain and snow)
variables.definition: How much rain and snow water reaches the ground, shown as the average amount per day over each month (millimeters of water per day).
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Precipitation only (rain and snow water), not a measure of soil wetness or river flow. Final Run is calibrated to monthly rain-gauge analyses where gauges exist, so the estimates perform best over land with many gauges and weaker over high latitudes, ice and snow, and steep terrain. The record joins the older TRMM-era and the GPM-era groups of satellites, so small steps are possible. Ocean cells are included.

variables.name: Aerosol optical depth (haze)
variables.definition: How much haze (dust, smoke and pollution particles) blocks sunlight in the whole air column above a place, at green light (550 nm). Near 0.05 is very clean air; above 0.5 is thick haze.
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Daytime, cloud-free views only: monthly means use only the days and places where the satellite could see the surface, and bright snow, ice and desert surfaces or persistent cloud give gaps. Aqua's afternoon overpass time has drifted later since July 2021 (NSIDC data announcement, 28 Oct 2021), so a small part of any change after 2021 can come from the changing view time and not from the air. Dark Target and Deep Blue retrievals are merged by NASA into one 550 nm value. AOD describes haze through the whole air column above a place, not the particles you breathe at ground level, so it is not the same as ground-level PM2.5.
variables.limits: Clear-sky only; AOD is a whole-column haze measure, not ground-level PM2.5; Aqua overpass drifts later after mid-2021, so months after Dec 2021 are flagged.
variables.quality_label: Aqua overpass drift: view time moves later
variables.quality_reason: Aqua's overpass time was steady until mid-2021 and then drifted later (NSIDC data announcement, 28 Oct 2021). A different view time and sun angle can shift the retrieved haze, so months after this date are flagged and left out by default. Our own check of Aqua view time (from the land surface temperature product, which shares the satellite) found no shift through 2021 and +0.05 h in 2022, growing to +0.9 h in 2025; the view time of this haze product itself is not in the monthly file.

variables.name: Terrestrial water storage anomaly
variables.definition: How much more or less water is stored on and under the ground than the 2004-2009 average, written as the height of a layer of water spread over the area (centimeters). Snow, ice, lakes, soil moisture and groundwater all count together.
variables.product: GRACE and GRACE-FO JPL mascons RL06.3 v04 (CRI)
variables.native_resolution: 0.5 degree grid (effective resolution about 3 degrees), block-averaged to 1 degree
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Total water storage anomaly, not groundwater alone: it adds up snow, ice, surface water, soil moisture and groundwater, and shows change relative to the 2004-2009 average, not an absolute amount. The satellites measure gravity over areas of roughly 300 km (about 3 degrees), so small regions are blurred and a 1-degree cell is not an independent measurement. There is a gap between GRACE (ended Jun 2017) and GRACE-FO (began Jun 2018) and a few single missing months; those are left empty, not filled. Solid-earth effects (glacial rebound) are removed by NASA's model, not measured.

variables.name: Land surface temperature (day)
variables.definition: How hot the ground surface is in the early afternoon, as seen from space on clear days, averaged over the month (degrees Celsius). It is hotter than the air temperature in sun-baked places.
variables.quality_label: Aqua overpass drift: reads too cool
variables.quality_reason: Aqua's overpass time was steady until 2021 and then drifted later, and a later daytime pass reads cooler. Months after this date are biased low, so they are left out by default and no verdict is given if you include them.
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Land surface temperature is the temperature of the ground and plant surface as seen from space (skin temperature), not the air temperature at weather stations, and it is only observed on clear-sky days, so cloudy places and seasons are under-sampled. Aqua passes at about 1:30 PM local time, so this is a mid-afternoon temperature, and Aqua's overpass time has drifted later since July 2021 (NSIDC 2021) while Terra, which we did not use for this library measurement, drifts earlier. Daytime only; ocean and water are not included; values are converted from kelvin to degrees Celsius once.

variables.name: Snow cover
variables.definition: The share of the ground (in percent) that the satellite saw covered by snow during the month, on days when it could see the ground.
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Percent of the ground that the satellite saw covered by snow on clear-sky days in the month, not snow depth or water content. Clouds hide the ground, and in polar night no data are collected, so high-latitude winter is empty. Terra's overpass time has drifted earlier since 2020 (NSIDC 2021), which can change snow-cover estimates slightly after 2020. Land only.

variables.name: Tropospheric nitrogen dioxide column
variables.definition: How much nitrogen dioxide (NO2, a brown gas made when fuel burns in cars, power plants and industry, and by lightning and fires) sits in the lower atmosphere above a spot, counted as molecules above each square centimeter of ground, in units of one thousand million million (10^15). City and industrial areas are the high spots.
variables.product: OMI/Aura OMNO2d v004 (cloud-screened Level-3 daily, averaged to monthly)
variables.native_resolution: 0.25 degree daily, averaged to monthly then block-averaged to 1 degree
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: A tropospheric column is all the NO2 gas in the lower atmosphere above a spot, counted as molecules per square centimeter (here in units of 10^15); it is not the concentration you breathe at street level. Cloud-screened: only scenes with cloud fraction at most 30% are kept (NASA's own screening), so cloudy places and seasons are under-sampled, and winter at high latitudes has few or no data. Since 2007 part of the OMI swath has been blocked (the 'row anomaly'); the NASA Level-3 product already drops affected pixels using its own quality flags, so coverage per day is smaller after 2007-2011 and the averages rest on fewer pixels. OMI passes at about 1:45 PM local time, so this is a mid-afternoon value, and NO2 has a strong daily and seasonal cycle. Monthly values here are the average of the daily cloud-screened grids, kept where at least 5 days are valid.
variables.limits: Column amount, not street-level NO2; cloud fraction at most 30% only; OMI row anomaly since 2007 shrinks daily coverage (affected pixels dropped by NASA's own quality flags); monthly cell kept only with at least 5 valid days; small negative values are retrieval noise and are kept, not clipped.

variables.name: Surface air temperature (day and night mean)
variables.definition: The temperature of the air near the ground, as estimated by an infrared sounder on the Aqua satellite, averaged over the afternoon and night passes and over the month (degrees Celsius). It works over land and ocean.
variables.product: AIRS/Aqua L3 monthly standard physical retrieval V7.0 (AIRS3STM)
variables.source_variable: SurfAirTemp_A and SurfAirTemp_D (K, mean of the two minus 273.15)
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Retrieved from the infrared sounder AIRS on Aqua together with microwave data, for scenes it can see through partly cloudy skies, so very cloudy places are under-sampled. The surface air temperature here is the mean of the afternoon (about 1:30 PM) and night (about 1:30 AM) overpasses, and is a retrieved value, not a weather-station reading. Aqua's overpass times have drifted later since July 2021 (NSIDC data announcement, 28 Oct 2021), which can shift both the day and night views a little after 2021. Version 7 replaces older versions, so do not splice with Version 6 values.

variables.name: Total water vapor column
variables.definition: How much water vapor (the invisible gas form of water) is in the whole column of air above a spot, written as the depth of liquid water it would make if it all condensed (millimeters). Warm, humid places have high values; cold, dry places have low ones.
variables.product: AIRS/Aqua L3 monthly standard physical retrieval V7.0 (AIRS3STM)
variables.source_variable: TotH2OVap_A and TotH2OVap_D (kg/m2, mean of the two)
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: Retrieved from the infrared sounder AIRS on Aqua together with microwave data, for scenes it can see through partly cloudy skies, so very cloudy places are under-sampled. The water vapor column here is the mean of the afternoon (about 1:30 PM) and night (about 1:30 AM) overpasses, and is a retrieved value, not a measurement from the ground. Aqua's overpass times have drifted later since July 2021 (NSIDC data announcement, 28 Oct 2021), which can shift both the day and night views a little after 2021. Version 7 replaces older versions, so do not splice with Version 6 values.

variables.name: Soil moisture, top 10 cm (model)
variables.definition: How much water the soil holds in its top 10 centimeters, written as millimeters of water (100 would be completely full). This is computed by a NASA land-surface model fed with satellite and ground weather data, not measured directly.
variables.units: kg/m2 (= mm of water in the top 10 cm)
variables.product: GLDAS Noah land surface model monthly V2.1 (GLDAS_NOAH10_M)
variables.kind: model output (land-surface model driven by observations)
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: MODEL OUTPUT, not a direct observation: the NASA GLDAS Noah land-surface model, driven by satellite- and ground-based weather inputs, computes how much water is in the top 10 cm of soil. It does not measure soil water from space. The value is the water in a 10 cm soil layer expressed as kg/m2 (the same as mm of water; 100 would mean completely full); frozen soil, forests and bare rock behave differently, and model biases can differ by region. Land only and only between 60S and 90N (no Antarctica). The forcing data changed over time in GLDAS 2.1, so check that a change is not just a change in the model inputs.

variables.name: Evapotranspiration (model)
variables.definition: How much water leaves the land and goes into the air each day, by evaporating from soil, puddles and leaves and by plants releasing water vapor (millimeters of water per day, monthly average). Computed by a NASA land-surface model, not measured directly.
variables.product: GLDAS Noah land surface model monthly V2.1 (GLDAS_NOAH10_M)
variables.kind: model output (land-surface model driven by observations)
variables.library_resolution: 1 degree, area-weighted block mean of valid native cells (block kept if >= 50% valid)
variables.caveats: MODEL OUTPUT, not a direct observation: the NASA GLDAS Noah land-surface model computes evapotranspiration (water leaving the land as evaporation from soil and water plus plant transpiration), in mm per day averaged over the month. It follows from the model's weather inputs and its vegetation and soil settings, so errors in rain or sunshine inputs carry through. Land only and only between 60S and 90N (no Antarctica). The forcing data changed over time in GLDAS 2.1, so check that a change is not just a change in the model inputs.
